cards.b:
Western theories of the state were built on European history. They do not fit well in countries that were colonies, like India, Pakistan or Nigeria.

Post-colonial theory asks: what kind of state did colonialism leave behind, and whom does it serve?

In his 1972 essay "The State in Post-Colonial Societies: Pakistan and Bangladesh", Alavi argued that the post-colonial state is "overdeveloped".

Colonial rulers built a powerful military-bureaucratic machine to control the whole colony. After independence, this machine stayed, and it was too strong for the weak local classes to control.

Alavi said three propertied classes exist in post-colonial societies: the metropolitan bourgeoisie (foreign capital), the indigenous bourgeoisie and the landed classes.

None dominates. So the military-bureaucratic oligarchy mediates between them and gains relative autonomy. This explains why the army so often rules in Pakistan.

Chatterjee, a key figure in Subaltern Studies, wrote Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986). He argued Indian nationalism borrowed Western ideas of the modern state even while opposing colonialism.

In The Politics of the Governed (2004), he separated civil society (a small elite of rights-bearing citizens) from political society (the majority, who deal with the state through welfare schemes and negotiation, not rights).

Rudolph and Rudolph

India's state is both strong and weak: strong in its reach, weak in delivering.

Gunnar Myrdal: the "soft state"

In Asian Drama (1968), he said South Asian states make good laws but cannot enforce them.

Dependency theory

Andre Gunder Frank and others argued post-colonial states stay economically dependent on the West.

• It can over-generalise. India stayed democratic while Pakistan saw coups; one theory struggles to explain both.
  • It can give colonialism too much weight and ignore local agency.
  • Developmental states like South Korea show post-colonial states can succeed economically.

cards.h: Other Indian readings of the state
cards.b:
Pranab Bardhan

In The Political Economy of Development in India (1984), he named three dominant proprietary classes: industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats. They compete for state subsidies, which slows growth.

Rajni Kothari

Described the decline of the Congress system and the rise of a more centralised, personalised state from the 1970s.

Atul Kohli

In State-Directed Development (2004), he called India a fragmented-multiclass state, less effective than South Korea's cohesive-capitalist state.

Sudipta Kaviraj

Read Indian state-building as a passive revolution led by bourgeois and bureaucratic elites.

India inherited the colonial machine almost whole: the IAS replaced the ICS, and the Indian Penal Code (1860) stayed in force until the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced it in 2024.

Yet India differs from Alavi's Pakistan. Regular elections, a strong Congress party in the early decades and firm civilian control kept the army out of politics.

Rudolph and Rudolph, in In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987), called this a weak-strong state. Chatterjee's political society shows the same thing at the ground level: the poor reach the state through negotiation, not through rights.

"Examine Hamza Alavi's concept of the overdeveloped state."
"Is the Indian state an overdeveloped state?"

Tip: use Alavi for the model, then test it on India. The Indian state was strong (overdeveloped) but civilian control and elections kept the army out, unlike Pakistan. That contrast earns marks.
